prompt: Starting in |0>, apply H then measure in the computational basis. Predict probabilities and distinguish them from finite-shot counts.
correct: P(0)=P(1)=1/2; finite counts need not split exactly equally.
incorrect: H guarantees exactly half zero and half one in every finite run.
partial: Both outcomes can occur, but I cannot specify their probabilities.
alternate: The two amplitudes have equal squared modulus, 1/2; shot counts fluctuate.
rationale: H creates equal-magnitude amplitudes; probabilities are not a guarantee about finite counts.

prompt: From |0>, run x(0); h(0). Explain the final state, including the relative sign and computational-basis probabilities.
correct: The state is (|0>-|1>)/sqrt(2). Each computational outcome has probability 1/2.
incorrect: The minus sign makes the probability of one negative.
partial: Both outcomes have probability 1/2; I have not identified the relative phase.
alternate: The second column of H has amplitudes +1/sqrt(2), -1/sqrt(2); squared magnitudes are equal.
rationale: A negative amplitude is permitted; probability is its squared magnitude. Phase is not recoverable from this histogram alone.

prompt: Fresh unaided exercise: |0> enters two consecutive H gates with no intermediate measurement. Predict the final measurement and explain why.
correct: Zero occurs with probability one because H squared is the identity.
incorrect: Two Hadamards give two independent coin flips so the final outcome is 50/50.
partial: The result is zero, but I cannot justify the cancellation.
alternate: Multiplying H by H cancels the |1> amplitude and restores |0>.
rationale: Coherent composition differs from measuring between gates. Matrix or amplitude reasoning is valid.

prompt: Select and justify: X acts on |0>. Is P(1) A: 0, B: 1/2, or C: 1? A selection alone does not supply the required justification.
correct: C: P(1)=1 because X exchanges the basis states.
incorrect: B: every quantum gate produces a fair random outcome.
alternate: X times the column vector (1,0) gives (0,1), so C.
rationale: X exchanges computational basis states; it does not generally randomise them.

prompt: Fresh unaided exercise: complete qc.x(0); qc.____(0) using X to return initial |0> to |0>. Explain the completed code.
correct: Use x. The second X flips |1> back to |0>.
incorrect: Use h. H always resets any qubit to zero.
partial: Use x, but no explanation is supplied.
alternate: Use x since the Pauli-X matrix is its own inverse.
rationale: Two X operations cancel coherently; H is not a reset operation.

prompt: For |0> followed by H then X, select all true statements and justify: A the final state is |+>; B P(1)=1; C both probabilities are 1/2.
correct: A and C. X exchanges two equal amplitudes and leaves |+> unchanged.
incorrect: B only: the last X forces every input state to |1>.
partial: C, because the counts look balanced; the state statement is omitted.
alternate: A,C: |+> is the +1 eigenvector of X, so the state is unchanged.
rationale: The effect of X depends on the input; the eigenstate explanation is an acceptable alternate approach.

prompt: Fresh unaided exercise: predict |0> after H, X, H without intermediate measurements. Explain the sequence.
correct: The final state is |0>: H makes |+>, X preserves it, and H maps it to |0>.
incorrect: The middle X guarantees a final one regardless of the last H.
partial: The result is zero; no intermediate-state explanation is supplied.
alternate: HXH is Z, and Z leaves initial |0> unchanged.
rationale: The Z identity is valid conceptual reasoning even though Z is outside the simulation gate allow-list.

prompt: Two qubits start at zero. Run x(0), measure q[i] to c[i]. Predict Qiskit's two-character output string and explain its order.
correct: 01; q0 is the rightmost bit in the displayed string.
incorrect: 10; q0 must be the leftmost character because it is drawn at the top.
partial: 01, with no explanation of the convention.
alternate: The displayed integer is 2^0=1, padded to two binary digits: 01.
rationale: Drawing order and displayed string order are distinct; explicit measurement mapping matters.

prompt: Fresh unaided exercise: two zero qubits, X on q1, identity measurement mapping. State the Qiskit output and justify.
correct: 10; q1 contributes the leftmost bit in this two-bit register.
incorrect: 01; all flipped qubits are printed on the right.
alternate: The classical value is 2^1=2, written as 10 in binary.
rationale: This fresh form changes which qubit is flipped while preserving the bit-order construct.

prompt: From |00>, apply H on q0 then CX with control q0 and target q1. Explain the state and why equal individual marginals do not mean independent outcomes.
correct: The state is (|00>+|11>)/sqrt(2). Each bit is balanced, but only matching pairs occur.
incorrect: Each qubit is 50/50, so all four joint strings are equally likely.
partial: Only 00 and 11 occur; the coherent state and independence distinction are missing.
alternate: CX maps the two input branches to 00 and 11; P(01)=0 differs from the product of marginals, 1/4.
rationale: The ideal circuit prepares a Bell state. A histogram alone does not distinguish this coherent state from a classical mixture.

prompt: From |00>, apply X to q1 then CX(q0,q1). Select and justify the final string: A 00, B 10, C 11, using q1q0 order.
correct: B: 10. The zero control q0 does not flip target q1.
incorrect: A: 00. CX always flips its target regardless of the control.
partial: B, but the control condition is unexplained.
alternate: Only the control-one subspace is exchanged by CX; this basis vector remains 10, so B.
rationale: CX is conditional. Control and target must not be silently swapped.

prompt: For |00> followed by H on each qubit, select and justify: A all four strings have probability 1/4; B the state is necessarily entangled; C it is a product of |+> states.
correct: A and C. Independent H gates make |+> tensor |+>, with equal probabilities for all four strings.
incorrect: B: any two superposed qubits are entangled.
partial: A; I have not explained whether the state factors.
alternate: A,C: the four amplitudes factor as (1,1)/sqrt(2) tensor (1,1)/sqrt(2).
rationale: Superposition is not sufficient for entanglement; factorisation establishes a product state.
